text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London closed sharply lower in a correction to Thursday's sharp rally to a twenty-month peak. The slide followed fund long liquidation as well as pre- weekend profit-taking. However, in spite of today's setback, the uptrend remains intact, due to tight supplies. The perception of robustas being well under-valued vis a vis arabicas attracted strong demand by roasters eager to step up use of robustas in the blends in order to help offset the steep arabica costs. The interest in second half 1997 robustas also spilled over to the cash market where it dominated business in major consuming countries. July closed $135 lower at $2,465 per tonne, while September gave up $130 to close at $2,500 per tonne.

Arabica futures' explosive three-day rally came to an abrupt halt, as frantic speculative selling sent the benchmark July contract plummeting 12 percent. July closed 38.40 cents/lb lower at 276.40 cents/lb. September gave up 35.50 cents/lb to close at 238.30 cents/lb.

The steep fall on Friday means that the market gave up a good portion of the gains made over the past three days. Traders said that while today's action might not be a premature end to the bull market, it will have shaken the confidence of many bulls and probably cause many to rethink and realign trading strategies even further. The spreads held up extremely well considering how the market sank.

There were two factors which were probably responsible for the interruption of the uptrend, even though they should not have come as a surprise. The first was the Man report that showed a large build up in consumer stocks which is not astonishing given the heavy shipments this year and secondly the symbolic gesture of the Colombian Coffee Federation to open current registrations. The times of tight supplies are not over yet and it can not be excluded that the market will soon resume its uptrend.

E.D.& F. MAN - World consumer stocks of green coffee stood at 10 million bags in April, up from 8.80 million bags in March and 1.1 million bags higher than in April 1996, UK trade house E.D.& F. Man said. Stocks at the end of April were 2.4 million bags above the all-time low of December 1996 of 7.6 million bags, reflecting some of the impact of high coffee imports earlier this year, Man said in its April/May coffee report. Man noted the growth in stocks had been less visible to the market as it had been concentrated in European ports. Bremen/Hamburg, the most important arabica ports in Europe, had now increased their stock holdings by 840,000 bags over the last two months, despite excellent roaster demand.

Man said the increase reflected the strength of coffee arrivals from Central America and Mexico. The European robusta ports had also increased their stock holdings. Antwerp stocks increased by nearly 200,000 bags in April due to a big increase in uncertified robusta coffee held in the port. US stocks had also increased by 309,000 bags in the last two months and by 198,000 bags in April alone to stand at 1.85 million bags.

COLOMBIA - The Colombian National Coffee Federation has authorized private exporters to ship coffee to the United States as part of the same measure that reopened 500,000 bags of May/June export registrations for Europe. The new measure also reopens June exports for Canada 'and other clients that traditionally buy Colombian coffee exclusively from private exporters'. However, one private exporter dismissed this new federation measure as nobody will buy coffee for June shipment, because the July/September spread in New York is extremely high and people prefer to buy against the September contract.

The federation remains silent so far on when it will open July registrations. The federation recently re-opened May/June export registrations to allow private exporters to sell 500,000 bags of coffee to the federation's clients in Europe and Japan. The federation had been unable to buy the coffee, which it needed to fulfill its export commitments under the ACPC retention scheme, acting general manager Heman Uribe said. The federation was unable to compete with the high prices private exporters were offering producers, according to trade sources.

SWEDEN - Sweden imported 136,800 bags of coffee in January 1997, 1 per cent less than was imported the same month the previous year. Total imports in calendar year 1996 reached 2.145 million bags, 30 per cent more than the 1.648 million bags imported the previous year. Main suppliers of green coffee in January 1997 were Brazil (42,100 vs 34,500 bags) and Colombia (36,000 vs 24,300 bags).

SWITZERLAND - Switzerland imported 94,033 bags of coffee in March 1997, 5 per cent more than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1997 up to 273,900 bags, 8 per cent more than was imported the same period in 1996. Total imports in calendar year 1996 rose by 7 percent to 1.121 million bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/March 1997 were Guatemala (21,700 vs 14,200 bags), Brazil (28,400 vs 22,400 bags) and Colombia (37,600 vs 50,400 bags). The country exported 70,100 bags of coffee in January/March 1997, 28 per cent more than was exported the same period in 1996. Total exports in calendar year 1996 rose by 33 percent to 245,000 bags.
